title: PFAS na nahuli sa activated carbon, puwedeng sirain ng laser? Japan team hits 99.999%+ in lab-stage test
summary: May bagong Japanese approach sa problemang kadalasang hindi natatapos sa filtration: pagkatapos ma-trap ang PFAS sa activated carbon, paano sisirain ang contaminant? Furukawa Electric at Ryuki Engineering report that a high-power fiber laser heated PFAS-loaded activated carbon above 1,100°C and achieved more than 99.999% degradation in evaluation tests. Promising ito, pero elemental technology pa lang—not yet a deployed municipal-water treatment system.
why_it_matters: Japan made PFOS/PFOA drinking-water limits mandatory in April 2026, so removal media itself becomes a downstream waste-treatment problem. A localized laser process could become another option for destroying PFAS captured on activated carbon, potentially without fully incinerating the carbon, but reuse, energy, throughput, by-products and economics still need real-world proof.

sources.publisher: Furukawa Electric Co., Ltd. / Ryuki Engineering Inc.
sources.title: Development of elemental technology for decomposition of PFAS using a high-power fiber laser
よくある質問 | 有機フッ素化合物（PFAS）について
溶融分離技術により3種類のPFAS（PFOS,PFOA,PFNA）を99.999%以上の高効率で分解

claims.text: Furukawa Electric and Ryuki Engineering reported PFAS degradation efficiency above 99.999% after irradiating PFAS-loaded activated carbon with a high-power fiber laser.
claims.basis: Joint company release describing the evaluation test and analytical measurement.

claims.text: The laser rapidly raised the target surface above 1,100°C; residual PFAS in solid and gas phases was collected and quantified by LC-MS/MS.
claims.basis: Published test method in the joint release.

claims.text: Japan has required compliance and testing for a combined PFOS/PFOA drinking-water standard of 50 ng/L or less since April 1, 2026.
A separate Kubota melting-process test reported above-99.999% destruction for PFOS, PFOA and PFNA, showing that high-temperature destruction is not unique to the laser approach.
The most interesting signal is not another PFAS filter but competition over the downstream destruction step after PFAS has been concentrated onto treatment media.
claims.basis: Both approaches address destruction of concentrated PFAS-bearing material rather than merely measuring or filtering PFAS.

claims.text: It is too early to assume the laser process will be cheaper, lower-carbon, scalable, or suitable for municipal water systems.
claims.basis: The companies describe this as elemental technology and future social implementation; commercial-scale operating data are not provided.

content.whats_new: 古河電工と流機エンジニアリングが、もともと鋼材のさび・塗膜除去に使う高出力ファイバレーザ技術をPFAS処理へ転用。PFASを吸着した活性炭を局所的に1,100°C超へ加熱し、評価試験で99.999%超の分解効率を報告した。
content.skeptical_view: Headline number is strong, pero lab/evaluation result ito. Walang published commercial throughput, kWh per kg, full lifecycle CO2, repeated activated-carbon reuse cycles, treatment cost, or municipal-scale operating record sa announcement. May competing high-temperature destruction routes na rin, including Kubota's melting process.
content.what_next: Watch for pilot-scale throughput, energy use, fluorinated by-products, carbon reuse performance, treatment cost per kg, and third-party/environmental validation under continuous operation.
content.what_would_change_mind: Mas magiging convincing ang case kapag may continuous pilot data, independent mass-balance/by-product testing, repeated activated-carbon reuse, at transparent energy and cost comparisons versus incineration or melting.
content.recommendation: WATCH — promising disposal/destruction technology, not a household action or proof that drinking-water PFAS is already solved.
content.bottom_line: May bagong candidate sa 'last mile' ng PFAS cleanup: hindi lang salain ang PFAS, kundi sirain ito pagkatapos ma-concentrate sa activated carbon. Maganda ang 99.999%+ test result, pero ang tunay na test ay scale, by-products, energy at cost.
